mainTopic: Lay judges in money cases, רבא and רב אחא on why three judges are needed, and why the משנה lists נזק and חצי נזק
overview: The amud opens by finishing רבי חנינא's teaching. By Torah law, money cases need the same careful questioning of witnesses (דרישה וחקירה) as capital cases. The חכמים relaxed this so lenders won't stop lending, and that is also why non-expert judges (הדיוטות) may judge loan cases. Even so, הדיוטות must pay if they make a mistake, because otherwise lenders would be scared off even more. The גמרא then shows two problems with רבי אבהו's reading of the משנה. In response, רבא explains that the משנה teaches two separate rules. רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says instead that by Torah law one judge is enough, and the חכמים required three because of יושבי קרנות. The practical difference between them is שמואל's rule that a court of two is valid but called a בית דין חצוף. Finally, the גמרא asks why the משנה lists 'damage' and 'half damage', tries the answer that half damage is a קנס, rejects it, and begins a new answer that continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The verse: one law for everyone
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא's statement continues. He brings his source that, by Torah law, money cases and capital cases are judged the same way.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'You shall have one law.'
steps.whatsHappening: This line finishes רבי חנינא's statement from just before. It gives the פסוק that proves money cases also need דרישה וחקירה by Torah law.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'one law' teach that all court cases are judged the same way. Capital cases clearly need careful questioning of witnesses, so by Torah law money cases need it too. This sets up the question that follows: why don't we actually do that?

keyTerms.meaning: One law, meaning one way of judging for all cases
As it says, which introduces a פסוק

phrases.english: As it says: 'You shall have one law.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes רבי חנינא's statement, which began just before this section, by giving its source.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law, money cases need דרישה וחקירה just like capital cases.

steps.title: Then why don't money cases need questioning of witnesses?
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא asks why the חכמים said money cases do not need careful questioning of witnesses.
steps.simpleTranslation: So why did the חכמים say that money cases don't need careful questioning of witnesses?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא asks an obvious question about his own rule, and this sets up his answer in the next step. If the Torah treats all cases the same, why don't we question witnesses in money cases?
steps.deeperAnalysis: In practice, money cases are judged without דרישה וחקירה. That looks like it goes against the Torah rule from the פסוק. So there must be a reason the חכמים relaxed it.

keyTerms.meaning: Careful questioning and cross-examining of witnesses
Money cases
We do not need

phrases.english: And what is the reason they said
that money cases do not need
questioning and cross-examination of witnesses?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks why actual practice differs from the Torah rule just proven.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The reason the חכמים waived דרישה וחקירה in money cases.

steps.title: So lenders will keep lending
steps.stepSummary: The reason is so that we don't 'lock the door' on people who need loans.
steps.simpleTranslation: So that you don't lock the door in front of borrowers.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא answers his question. The rule was relaxed so lenders would not be afraid to lend money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If every loan case needed full questioning of witnesses, it would be very hard for a lender to win in court. Lenders would stop lending, and poor people could not get loans. The same reason explains why non-expert judges (הדיוטות) are allowed in loan cases.

keyTerms.meaning: Locking the door, meaning blocking people from getting loans
Borrowers

steps.whatToRemember: The rule is called נעילת דלת. The חכמים made money cases easier to judge so that lenders won't stop lending.
steps.whyThisMatters: This one reason explains why money cases are relaxed in more than one way: no questioning of witnesses and no need for expert judges.

phrases.english: So that you do not lock the door
in front of borrowers.

steps.triggerLanguage: כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא תִּנְעוֹל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לוֹוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The חכמים relaxed the rules so lenders would not be scared away from lending.

steps.title: Should non-expert judges then not pay for mistakes?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: if הדיוטות are allowed for the lenders' sake, maybe when they make a mistake they shouldn't have to pay, just like expert judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then if they make a mistake, they shouldn't have to pay?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the idea that הדיוטות fully count as proper judges. If they do, then like an expert judge, they should not have to pay when they rule wrongly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The challenge assumes that an expert judge (מומחה) who makes a mistake does not pay. If the חכמים gave הדיוטות a judge's power, maybe they also get that protection. The challenge asks how far the special treatment of הדיוטות goes.

keyTerms.meaning: But if so, now that you said this
They made a mistake in judgment
They will pay

phrases.english: But if so,
if they made a mistake, they should not pay?!
phrases.notes: 'They' means the non-expert judges, who would then be just like an expert judge, who doesn't pay.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the נעילת דלת reason and pushes it further, to the question of paying for mistakes.
steps.kashyaTarget: The status of הדיוטות who are allowed to judge because of נעילת דלת
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If they count as real judges, they should be free from paying for mistakes, just like experts.

steps.title: No, that would scare lenders even more
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that freeing הדיוטות from paying would make the problem much worse.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the more so you would be locking the door in front of borrowers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers using the same reason. If mistaken הדיוטות didn't pay, lenders would fear losing their money and would stop lending.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Making הדיוטות pay for their mistakes protects lenders. Freeing them from paying would hurt the very lenders the rule was made to help. So the same reason that lets הדיוטות judge also means they must pay when they make a mistake.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so

steps.whatToRemember: הדיוטות may judge loan cases, but if they make a mistake they must pay. Both rules come from the same reason: protecting lenders.

phrases.english: All the more so you are locking the door
in front of borrowers!

steps.triggerLanguage: כׇּל שֶׁכֵּן אַתָּה נוֹעֵל דֶּלֶת בִּפְנֵי לוֹוִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge of step 4 by using its own reason against it.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Turns the challenger's own reason around
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since הדיוטות were allowed in order to help lenders, maybe they are protected like experts.
steps.terutzMaskana: The goal of protecting lenders requires that הדיוטות pay for their mistakes.

steps.title: The משנה should have openly said 'two rules'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי אבהו: if loans need only הדיוטות and robbery needs experts, the משנה should have stated these as two separate rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, the משנה is teaching two things: money cases are judged by three non-experts, and robbery and injury cases by three experts.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to רבי אבהו's reading of the משנה and challenges it. It says the משנה should simply have listed two separate rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אבהו read 'גזילות וחבלות' as an explanation of 'דיני ממונות', meaning 'what does this include?'. But if loan cases really need only הדיוטות while robbery and injury need experts, these are two different laws. The משנה should have said so plainly.

keyTerms.meaning: If so
It teaches two things
Non-expert, unordained judges
Expert, ordained judges
Robbery and injury cases

phrases.english: If so, it should teach two things:
money cases are judged by three non-experts,
robbery and injury cases are judged by three experts.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the side discussion about paying for mistakes back to רבי אבהו's reading of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's reading of 'גזילות וחבלות' as an explanation of 'דיני ממונות'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the two kinds of cases have different laws, the משנה should have stated them as two separate rules instead of one rule plus an explanation.

steps.title: Why say 'three' twice?
steps.stepSummary: A second challenge to רבי אבהו: saying 'three' twice shows that these are two separate rules.
steps.simpleTranslation: And also, why do I need 'three' and 'three'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another problem with רבי אבהו's reading. The משנה says 'three' for each case separately.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the second part were only explaining the first, the משנה would not need to say 'three judges' again. The repeated 'three' points to two independent rules. That goes against reading it as one rule with an explanation.

keyTerms.meaning: And also, adding a further challenge
Why do I need it?

steps.confusionAlert: Both cases need three judges. The challenge is not about how many judges. It is about why the משנה repeats the number if the two cases are really one rule.

phrases.english: And also, why do I need 'three' and 'three'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second challenge to רבי אבהו, alongside step 6.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי אבהו's reading of the משנה as a single rule
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Repeating 'three' only makes sense if the משנה is giving two separate rules.

steps.title: רבא: The משנה Teaches Two Rules
steps.stepSummary: רבא accepts that the משנה contains two separate rules. Non-experts are allowed in loan cases because of רבי חנינא's reason.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: The משנה is teaching two separate rules, because of what רבי חנינא said.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the challenges against רבי אבהו worked, רבא gives a new explanation. Yes, the משנה is teaching two separate rules.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 6–7 proved that the משנה's wording points to two rules. רבא agrees with that and explains why loans are different. As רבי חנינא said, we don't want to 'lock the door' on borrowers, so non-expert judges are allowed for loans.

keyTerms.meaning: It is teaching two (separate rules)
Rather (drops the earlier approach and starts a new one)
The אמורא who gave the reason of not locking the door on borrowers

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
It teaches two [separate rules],
because of [the teaching] of Rabbi Chanina.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Accepts the point of the challenges in steps 6–7 and gives a new reading of the משנה.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation: accept the challenger's reading and give it a new reason
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי אבהו: the משנה teaches one combined rule about how many judges are needed
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה teaches two separate rules, and non-experts are allowed in loan cases because of רבי חנינא's reason

steps.title: רב אחא: One Judge Is Valid by Torah Law
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב איקא says that by Torah law one judge is enough. The רבנן required three because of יושבי קרנות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא, son of רב איקא, said: By Torah law even one judge is valid, as the פסוק says 'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.' Three are required only because of people who sit idly on street corners.
steps.whatsHappening: A second אמורא gives a completely different explanation for why three judges are needed. He says it is a rabbinic rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק speaks to one person ('you judge'), which shows that a single judge is valid by Torah law. The רבנן required three because a single judge might be an unlearned idler who would get the case wrong.

keyTerms.meaning: By Torah law
'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor' (singular)
Those who sit on street corners: unlearned idlers

steps.whyThisMatters: It turns the requirement of three judges from a Torah law into a rabbinic safeguard. This sets up the practical difference shown later in step 15.

phrases.aramaic: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר:
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Ika said:
By Torah law, even one [judge] is valid,
as it says: 'In righteousness shall you judge your neighbor.'
phrases.notes: ויקרא 19:15. 'You judge' is said to one person.

phrases.english: But [three are required] because of those who sit on street corners.
phrases.notes: These are unlearned, idle people who don't know how business works, so they might judge badly.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different explanation next to רבא's.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: By Torah law one judge is valid. The רבנן required three so that unlearned idlers will not judge alone.

steps.title: Can't Three Judges Also Be Idlers?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how having three judges solves the problem, since all three could be unlearned.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that to say that with three judges, they won't be street-corner idlers?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אחא's reasoning. Adding more judges doesn't seem to guarantee that they are learned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the worry is unlearned judges, three unlearned people are no better than one. So why should the number of judges fix the problem?

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say...? (introduces a challenge)
With three

phrases.english: Is that to say that with three
there won't be street-corner sitters?

steps.triggerLanguage: אַטּוּ בִּתְלָתָא מִי לָא הָווּ יוֹשְׁבֵי קְרָנוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reasoning of step 9.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב אחא's claim that three judges solve the problem of יושבי קרנות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Three people can be unlearned just as easily as one, so the number of judges doesn't seem to help.

steps.title: Among Three, One Will Be Learned
steps.stepSummary: With three judges, it is almost certain that at least one knows the law.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is impossible that there isn't one learned person among them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא defends רב אחא. In a group of three, at least one will almost surely know what he is doing.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is not that all three will be learned. The point is that one learned judge among them will guide the others to the right ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: It is impossible (here: very unlikely otherwise)
Who is learned

phrases.english: It is impossible
that there isn't among them one who is learned.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי אֶפְשָׁר דְּלֵית בְּהוּ חַד דִּגְמִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 10.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Three judges could all be unlearned
steps.terutzMaskana: Among three, at least one will almost surely be learned

steps.title: Then Shouldn't Mistaken Judges Be Free from Paying?
steps.stepSummary: If laymen are allowed to judge, maybe they shouldn't have to pay when they make a mistake.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, when they make a mistake, should they not have to pay?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אחא's view the same way it challenged an earlier view in step 4. Since the רבנן allowed these laymen to judge, maybe they shouldn't be held responsible for mistakes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Expert judges who are authorized do not pay for honest mistakes. If the system was set up for laymen to judge, perhaps they should get the same protection.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, then... (introduces a troubling result)
They made a mistake
They must pay

steps.confusionAlert: This looks like a repeat of step 4, but it is a new challenge. This time the question is aimed at רב אחא's explanation.

phrases.english: If so,
if they err, they should not pay?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second challenge to רב אחא's approach.
steps.kashyaTarget: The liability of lay judges under רב אחא's view
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the רבנן authorized laymen, they should be exempt from paying for mistakes, the same as authorized experts.

steps.title: Exempting Them Would Bring More Idlers
steps.stepSummary: Freeing lay judges from paying would make many more unqualified people want to judge.
steps.simpleTranslation: All the more so would there be many street-corner idlers!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that if mistakes cost nothing, even more unqualified people would rush to be judges.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Having to pay for mistakes keeps careless people away. Removing it would undo the whole reason the רבנן required three judges.

keyTerms.meaning: All the more so
That they would increase / become many

steps.whatToRemember: According to רב אחא, three judges are a rabbinic safeguard so that one will be learned. Lay judges still pay for mistakes, to keep unqualified people from judging.

phrases.english: All the more so
would street-corner sitters multiply!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Policy reasoning: the change would defeat the purpose of the rule
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Authorized lay judges should be exempt from paying for mistakes
steps.terutzMaskana: Exempting them would invite even more unqualified judges, so they must pay

steps.title: What Is the Difference Between רבא and רב אחא?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what practical difference there is between the two explanations.
steps.simpleTranslation: What difference is there between רבא and רב אחא, son of רב איקא?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא sets up the next move by asking whether these two views lead to different practical results.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both explanations allow three laymen to judge loan cases. The גמרא wants to know where they would actually rule differently.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the difference between...?

phrases.english: What is [the difference] between Rava
and Rav Acha son of Rav Ika?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי אִיכָּא בֵּין רָבָא לְרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Compares the two approaches given in steps 8 and 9.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The practical difference between רבא's and רב אחא's explanations

steps.title: The Difference: שמואל's Court of Two
steps.stepSummary: They disagree about שמואל's ruling that a court of two is valid but called 'impudent.' רב אחא agrees with it, and רבא does not.
steps.simpleTranslation: The difference between them is what שמואל said: If two people judged a case, their ruling counts, but they are called an impudent court. רבא does not hold like שמואל. רב אחא, son of רב איקא, does hold like שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that the two views split on whether a ruling by only two judges is valid.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב אחא, even one judge is valid by Torah law, so a court of two certainly is. They are only criticized for not having three. רבא holds that three are needed at the Torah level, so a court of two is not valid.

keyTerms.meaning: There is a difference between them
Their ruling is a valid ruling
An impudent (brazen) court
He holds / does not hold (this view)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא: three judges are needed by Torah law, so two cannot judge. רב אחא: one is enough by Torah law, so two can judge (as שמואל says), but they are called a בית דין חצוף.

phrases.english: There is [a difference] between them
regarding what Shmuel said:
Two who judged, their judgment is a [valid] judgment,
except that they are called an impudent court.
phrases.notes: They were bold enough to judge without the usual third judge.

phrases.english: Rava does not hold like Shmuel,

phrases.aramaic: לְרַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב אִיקָא אִית לֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל.
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Ika holds like Shmuel.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: They differ on שמואל's rule. רב אחא accepts that a court of two is valid, and רבא rejects it.

steps.title: Isn't 'Damage' the Same as 'Injuries'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the משנה's words 'damage and half damage' and asks why 'damage' is listed when 'injuries' seem to cover it.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'Damage and half damage, etc.' But isn't 'damage' the same as 'injuries'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new phrase in the משנה. It asks why full damage is listed separately, since it seems to be included in 'injuries.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה already said that cases of injuries need three judges. Listing 'damage' as well looks like it says the same thing twice.

keyTerms.meaning: Damage (full payment)
Half damage (half payment, as with a תם ox)
Injuries
That is the same as

phrases.english: [The Mishnah said:] Damage and half damage, etc.
Isn't damage the same as injuries?

steps.triggerLanguage: נֶזֶק וַחֲצִי נֶזֶק וְכוּ׳ נֶזֶק הַיְינוּ חֲבָלוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic on a different phrase of the משנה.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: 'Damage' already seems to be covered by 'injuries,' so listing it is extra.

steps.title: Full Damage Is Listed Alongside Half Damage
steps.stepSummary: The משנה mentioned full damage only because it wanted to teach half damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because the משנה wanted to teach half damage, it also taught full damage.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains that 'full damage' is there only to go with 'half damage,' which is the new point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Half damage is the part that teaches something new. Full damage was written next to it so the list reads naturally, even though 'injuries' already covers it.

keyTerms.meaning: Because it wanted to teach
Full damage

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּקָא בָּעֵי לְמִיתְנֵא חֲצִי נֶזֶק,
phrases.english: Because it wanted to teach half damage,
it also taught full damage.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּקָא בָּעֵי לְמִיתְנֵא חֲצִי נֶזֶק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 16.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Stylistic: the extra item is mentioned only to go with the new one
steps.terutzMaskana: Full damage is listed only alongside half damage, which is the real new point

steps.title: Isn't half damage the same as injuries?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges: 'half damage' also seems covered by 'injuries,' so why list it separately?
steps.simpleTranslation: Half damage is also the same as injuries!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא carries the same question one step further. It now asks why the משנה needs to mention 'half damage,' since 'injuries' seems to cover it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 17 the גמרא said 'damage' was listed only to set up 'half damage.' That answer assumes 'half damage' itself needs to be said. Now the גמרא challenges that assumption: half damage is also a kind of harm, so 'injuries' (חבלות) should already include it.

keyTerms.meaning: Half damage: a payment of half the value of the harm caused
Injuries: the משנה's word for harm-related monetary cases
That is the same as

phrases.english: Half damage, too,
is the same as injuries!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Pushes the redundancy question from 'damage' (Step 16) onto 'half damage,' which Step 17's answer depended on.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's separate listing of חצי נזק
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If חבלות already covers harm cases, then חצי נזק adds nothing. Step 17's answer, which needs חצי נזק to be a real teaching, would then fall apart.

steps.title: Half damage is a fine, not ordinary money
steps.stepSummary: The משנה taught money cases and then also taught a fine, which is half damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: The תנא taught a money case, and he also teaches a fine.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that half damage is different from injuries. Injuries are ordinary money payments, while half damage is a fine (קנס).
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since a fine is a different legal category from regular money, the משנה had to tell us that fines are also judged by three. So 'half damage' is not redundant. It teaches a new kind of case.

keyTerms.meaning: Money: a regular payment for a loss actually caused
A fine: a penalty payment set by the Torah, not exact repayment of a loss
He (the author of the משנה) taught

phrases.english: He taught a money case,
and he also teaches a fine.
phrases.notes: The fine here is the half damage itself.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 18 by putting חצי נזק in a separate category (קנס) from חבלות.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Category distinction: fine versus ordinary money
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חצי נזק is just another harm payment, already included in חבלות.
steps.terutzMaskana: חצי נזק is a קנס, so the משנה lists it to show that fines are also judged by three.

steps.title: That answer only works if half damage is a fine
steps.stepSummary: The fine answer works only for the opinion that half damage is a fine. For the opinion that it is regular money, the question comes back.
steps.simpleTranslation: This works well according to the one who says half damage is a fine. But according to the one who says half damage is money, what can be said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks its own answer. It points out that there is a known argument over whether half damage is a fine or a regular money payment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If half damage counts as ordinary money (ממון), it belongs in the same category as injuries. Then the answer from Step 19 fails, and 'half damage' looks redundant again. The phrase 'what can be said?' shows that this answer is being dropped.

keyTerms.meaning: This works out well (for one opinion)
Half damage (Aramaic for חצי נזק)
What can be said? A sign that the answer does not hold

steps.confusionAlert: This step does not decide whether half damage is a fine or money. It only shows that the answer in Step 19 cannot work for both opinions, so the גמרא needs an answer that works for everyone.

phrases.english: This works well according to the one who says:
'Half damage is a fine,'
but according to the one who says:
'Half damage is money,'
what can be said?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָנִיחָא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא קְנָסָא אֶלָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר פַּלְגָא נִיזְקָא מָמוֹנָא מַאי אִיכָּא לְמֵימַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges Step 19 by showing it depends on one side of a dispute.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that חצי נזק is listed because it is a קנס
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Under the view פלגא נזקא ממונא, חצי נזק is ordinary money like חבלות, so the category distinction disappears and the redundancy comes back.

steps.title: New answer: half damage is listed because of the double and four-or-five payments
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא begins a new answer: since the משנה wanted to teach double payment and four-or-five payment, it also listed half damage.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, since he wanted to teach double payment and four-or-five payment, which are money...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops the fine answer and starts a new explanation based on the next items in the משנה's list. The sentence is not finished here; it continues in the next lines.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'rather' (אלא) means a fresh answer that has to work for everyone. The new answer connects 'half damage' to the double payment and four-or-five payment that come right after it in the משנה. The full reason is finished in the next part of the text.

keyTerms.meaning: Since / because (the משנה) was already going to
Double payment: what a thief pays when caught
Four or five times payment: for stealing and then slaughtering or selling a sheep or an ox

phrases.english: Rather, since he wanted to teach
double payment
and four-or-five payment,
which are money...

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אַיְּידֵי דְּקָא בָּעֵי לְמִיתְנֵא תַּשְׁלוּמֵי כֶּפֶל וְתַשְׁלוּמֵי אַרְבָּעָה וַחֲמִשָּׁה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer rejected in Step 20 with a new answer to Step 18's question.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Listing because of what comes next (איידי)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: חצי נזק must teach its own new category, or else it is redundant.
steps.terutzMaskana: The answer is still in progress: חצי נזק is listed because of the כפל and ד' וה' payments that follow it. The reasoning is finished in the next lines.
